Ghusl and the
return to prayer
5 min read
Guide
Beginner
Reviewed content
The general steps for resuming prayer after menstruation, with peace of mind.
Important information
This content is purely educational. Religious questions should be validated by qualified scholars. AWA does not issue fatwas or personalized religious rulings.
In this article
Ghusl, return to ritual purity
A method that can vary by school
Resuming prayer, without making up missed prayers
Practical points to remember

Ghusl is a major ritual ablution: it consists of washing the entire body with the intention of returning to the state of ritual purity (tahara), necessary for performing prayer and other acts of worship.

Before performing the ghusl, it’s important to make sure that menstruation has truly ended: the ghusl should follow, not precede, the certainty that the bleeding has stopped. Generally speaking, this end is recognized by the total stopping of bleeding, observed over a sufficient period of time to rule out any doubt — a point covered in detail in the article dedicated to ritual purity.
This purification is what allows you to reconnect with the moments of worship suspended during menstruation.
Good to know
There’s no need to feel rushed: the ghusl can be performed as soon as you’re ready, without pressure, once the end of menstruation has been confirmed with certainty.

The ghusl is based on shared general principles: the intention to purify oneself, and the complete washing of the body, including the hair and skin. The precise details of the method, however, can vary according to the school of jurisprudence followed.
Important note

No particular method is presented here as the only valid one: referring to the school or opinion you usually follow, or seeking advice from a qualified scholar, will help you learn the precise details suited to your situation.
Once menstruation has ended and the ghusl has been performed, prayer resumes normally, with no particular delay or additional condition.

It’s helpful to distinguish between two situations that follow different rules: prayers not performed during menstruation are generally not made up, whereas fasting days missed during Ramadan must be made up later (qadaa).

For example, a woman who has had her period for 6 days resumes prayer normally after the ghusl, without having to make up the prayers from those 6 days. The corresponding 6 days of fasting, however, will be made up after Ramadan.

SIDE EFFECTS

Recognizing possible
side effects

Article
Intermediate
Reviewed content
Some effects can be common and temporary. Others need more attention. Learn to tell the difference between usual reactions and signs that should be evaluated.
In this article
Common, mild effects
The body’s adjustment period
Observing what changes
When to seek medical advice
When to seek care quickly
Key takeaways
When someone starts a new hormonal contraception method, the body may need some time to adjust. Small changes can appear in the cycle, mood, or physical comfort.
These effects are often mild and may gradually decrease. Their presence doesn’t automatically mean the method is dangerous or that it needs to be stopped.
Minor bleeding
Irregular bleeding can occur, especially at the start of a new method.
Breast tenderness
Breast tightness or tenderness may be felt temporarily.
Mood
Some people notice mood changes or increased emotional sensitivity.
Headaches
Mild headaches can occur during the adjustment period.
The first few weeks or cycles may be different from what you were used to before. The body can gradually adjust to the new hormonal balance.
Good to know
An effect that appears shortly after starting a method is worth watching over time. If it becomes bothersome or persists, talk to a healthcare professional.
It can be helpful to log symptoms in your app to better track how they change from one cycle to the next.
Track how things evolve
A few markers can be helpful
Note the date the symptom appeared.
Record its intensity and duration.
Watch whether it improves or worsens.
Not all symptoms are necessarily linked to contraception. Stress, sleep, diet, your cycle, or other treatments can also affect how you feel.
To understand the situation, try to look at the overall context rather than a single symptom in isolation.
Marked, persistent mood changes
A drop in libido that bothers you
Irregular bleeding that lasts more than 3 cycles
Nausea or headaches that remain bothersome
A few helpful questions
How long have these symptoms been going on?
Did they appear after starting or changing a contraception method?
Are they mild, bothersome, or truly unusual for you?
Are they improving over time or becoming more frequent?
Even when a symptom isn’t urgent, it can be worth discussing it if it becomes bothersome, persists, or genuinely affects your quality of life.
It may be worth getting advice if…
symptoms persist, become more significant, or keep you from living normally.
A doctor, midwife, or pharmacist can help you determine whether the symptoms may be linked to the method you’re using and whether it needs to be adjusted.
Some signs are unusual and call for prompt medical evaluation. They don’t necessarily mean a complication is present, but they should not be ignored.
Seek care quickly
Seek medical advice quickly if you experience, in particular:
Significant or unusual chest pain
Sudden difficulty breathing
Unusual swelling or pain in a leg
A sudden, very intense, or unusual headache
Sudden trouble with vision, speech, or strength
In case of a severe situation
If symptoms are sudden, very severe, or come with difficulty breathing, feeling faint, or another serious sign, seek urgent medical help.
The essentials
Some effects can appear at the start of a new hormonal contraception method.
Many effects are temporary and may decrease over time.
A bothersome or persistent symptom is worth discussing with a professional.
Some unusual signs require prompt medical advice.
Key takeaway
Listening to your body doesn’t necessarily mean stopping a method right away. Note what you’re feeling, watch how it evolves, and ask for advice whenever a symptom concerns you.
This article is intended for information purposes and does not replace personalized medical advice. If you have a significant or unusual symptom, seek advice from a healthcare professional.

Sleep and hormones:
the little-known link

Why your sleep changes depending on your cycle phase, and at menopause.
In this article
Why hormones affect sleep
Sleep across the phases of the cycle
Stress and sleep quality
A soothing evening routine
When to see a professional
Key takeaways
Progesterone has a mild sedative effect; its drop at the end of the cycle can disrupt sleep, making it lighter or more fragmented.
Good to know
The slight rise in body temperature after ovulation can also make falling asleep a little harder for some people.
During your period
Physical discomfort and fatigue can make sleep lighter.
Around ovulation
Sleep is generally more stable for most people.
Before your period
The drop in progesterone can make sleep lighter, with possible wake-ups.
At menopause, night sweats are a common cause of waking up, for similar hormonal reasons.
Stress can amplify sleep disruptions during phases of the cycle that are already more sensitive. Simple relaxation techniques (breathing, gentle stretching) can help you unwind before bed.
A stable bedtime routine and a cool bedroom help limit these disruptions, at any age.
Regular hours
Going to bed and waking up at stable times helps regulate your internal clock.
Less screen time in the evening
Blue light can delay falling asleep; a screen break helps you wind down.
A cool bedroom
A moderate temperature makes falling asleep easier, at any age.
Good habits aren’t always enough. It can be helpful to talk to a professional if:
Signs worth getting checked
Sleep problems have lasted for several weeks
Fatigue is strongly affecting daily life
Insomnia persists despite good habits
Preparing for this appointment
Noting how long the problems have lasted and what seems to influence them can help your healthcare professional guide you better.
Good to know
These sleep changes are common and usually temporary: they don’t mean something is wrong.
Progesterone has a mild sedative effect; its drop at the end of the cycle can disrupt sleep.
At menopause, night sweats are a common cause of waking up.
A stable bedtime routine and a cool bedroom help limit these disruptions, at any age.
Persistent sleep problems are worth discussing with a healthcare professional.
Informational content. This article does not replace personalized medical advice. If in doubt, seek guidance from a healthcare professional.

Understanding your period:
what’s really happening
5 min read
Reviewed content
Your period is part of a natural process that’s essential to hormonal and reproductive health. Understanding what’s happening in your body can help you feel more at ease with each cycle.
In this article
What is a period?
How your period unfolds
What’s normal (and what isn’t)
Relieving pain naturally
A period is the shedding of the uterine lining when no fertilization has occurred. This happens on average once a month.
Good to know
Every woman is unique: duration, intensity, and sensations can vary from one cycle to the next.
Flow isn’t the same throughout your period. It usually changes from day to day, in intensity, color, and texture.
Start of your period
Flow is often heavier during the first few days.
Middle of your period
Flow generally starts to gradually decrease.
End of your period
Flow becomes lighter and may take on a darker color.
Keep in mind
This can vary from one cycle to another. What matters most is knowing your own usual rhythm.
Some variations are common during your period. Other signs deserve more attention, especially when they’re new or very intense.
Duration
A period that usually lasts a few days.
Varying flow
Heavier flow at first, then lighter.
Color
From bright red to dark red or brown toward the end of your period.
Sensations
Mild to moderate cramps may be felt.
When to seek medical advice?
Very intense or unusual pain
Bleeding that soaks through a pad or tampon very quickly
Significant fatigue, feeling faint, or dizziness
A sudden and persistent change from your usual pattern
Simple habits can help ease discomfort and make the first days of your period more comfortable.

limit fatigue.

abdomen if needed.

activity: walking,
yoga, stretching.

vaginal ring

A flexible ring, worn for three weeks.
In this article
How the ring works
Insertion and removal
What you need to know
Key takeaways
The ring is a flexible device that continuously releases low doses of hormones directly in the vagina, with the same contraceptive action as a combined pill.
How it works
Ring
Placed in the vagina
Hormones
Continuous diffusion
Protection
Contraceptive action
You insert it yourself, it stays in place continuously for three weeks, then it’s removed for a one-week break during which your period occurs.
A simple rhythm to follow
Ring
Break
Week with the ring
Break week
Good to know
Its exact position in the vagina doesn’t need to be precise for it to be effective, which makes it simple to use.
The ring has several practical points worth knowing before choosing it.
Simple to use
You insert and remove it yourself.
Regular rhythm
It generally stays in place for three weeks.
Continuous action
Hormones are released continuously throughout the period of use.
Doesn’t protect against STIs
Additional protection may be needed depending on the situation.
Good habits to keep
Wash your hands before inserting or removing it
Choose a time that’s easy to remember to keep track of the schedule
Occasionally check that it’s still in place
Check the leaflet if it shifts or is expelled
Please note
An expulsion or prolonged displacement may require specific guidance. Always check the device’s leaflet or ask a healthcare professional if you’re unsure.
The essentials in 4 points
Simple insertion
The ring can be inserted and removed by yourself.
Weekly rhythm
It generally follows a three-week cycle with a one-week break.
Occasional check
Checking regularly that it’s in place helps you use the device with peace of mind.
No protection against STIs
Suitable protection may be needed depending on the situation.
Key takeaways

The vaginal ring combines continuous hormone release with a usage rhythm that avoids a daily dose. However, the choice of contraception should be tailored to each person and discussed with a healthcare professional.

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of your last period, by medical convention. At this stage, fertilization has generally not yet taken place.
This period generally comes before conception; there usually isn’t yet any pregnancy-related physical change.
Counting pregnancy from the last period gives a standardized way of estimating a due date, even though conception actually happens a bit later.
It’s common not to notice any change at this stage.
Ovulation and possible fertilization generally occur around this time, depending on each person’s cycle length.
The timing of ovulation can vary depending on cycle length, which affects the actual possible date of conception.
There is generally no pregnancy-specific physical change yet at this stage.
The exact timing of ovulation varies from person to person, which is why this period remains an estimate.
If fertilization has occurred, the egg begins dividing and moving toward the uterus, but nothing is detectable yet by a pregnancy test.
This week still falls within the medical dating period surrounding conception; no physical sign is generally noticeable at this stage.
Most urine pregnancy tests become reliable from around the following week, once implantation has begun.
The embryo has just implanted in the uterine wall. The amniotic sac and the yolk sac, which will nourish it in the very first days, are forming.
